Can a Power Station Run an Electric Blanket?
AR

Alejandro Rodríguez, MD
Physician (MD, Colombia)

Sep 24, 2026
Sep 25, 2026

Specs verified, runtimes calculated. We don’t lab-test power stations (yet). How we research

Yes, and it is one of the most efficient ways to stay warm on battery power.
The U.S. Department of Energy lists typical electric blankets at about 60 W for a single and 100 W for a double, and Sunbeam rates its current full-size heated blankets at 110 W. At 100 W, a 1,024 Wh power station runs the blanket for about 8 hours, roughly one night, and a 2,048 Wh unit for about 16 hours. A 1,500 W space heater would empty the same 1 kWh unit in about 35 minutes.

How we got these numbers: we use published wattage ratings and our standard runtime math, not hands-on measurements. We plan on each blanket’s full rated watts; on lower settings most blankets draw less, so your real runtime is usually longer. See How We Research.

How many watts an electric blanket uses
Blanket	Rated watts	Source
Single (typical)	About 60 W	U.S. Department of Energy
Double (typical)	About 100 W	U.S. Department of Energy
Sunbeam full-size heated blanket	110 W	Sunbeam product listing
Queen or king with two controllers (example)	About 200 W if both sides run at 100 W	Add the watts on both controller labels

The number on the controller or the tag is the maximum. Queen and king blankets usually have two controllers, one per side, so add both labels. Blankets cycle their heat to hold the setting, which is why the real average on a low or medium setting is usually below the label.

How long a power station runs an electric blanket

Formula: hours = (power station Wh × 0.85) ÷ (blanket watts + 10)

Try your own numbers

Battery size (Wh)
Device average watts
7.7 h
1,000 Wh x 0.85 / (100 W + 10 W). An estimate: check that the unit’s AC output covers your device.
Find the blanket’s watts on the label. Example: 100 W.
Add 10 W for the power station’s inverter: 110 W.
Multiply the battery by 0.85 for usable energy. For a 1,024 Wh unit: 1,024 × 0.85 = about 870 Wh.
Divide: 870 ÷ 110 = about 7.9 hours.
Blanket (rated watts)	286 Wh (small)	1,024 Wh	2,048 Wh
Single, 60 W	About 3.5 hours	About 12 hours	About 25 hours
Double, 100 W	About 2.2 hours	About 7.9 hours	About 16 hours
Full, 110 W	About 2 hours	About 7.3 hours	About 14.5 hours
Queen, both sides, 200 W	About 1.2 hours	About 4.1 hours	About 8.3 hours
For comparison: 1,500 W space heater	Cannot run it	About 35 minutes	About 1.2 hours

These are full-power figures, so treat them as the minimum. Plug in your own mix of devices with our power station calculator.

Why a blanket beats a space heater on battery

A space heater tries to warm the air in a whole room, and the heat leaks out through windows and walls. A blanket puts a small amount of heat right where you are. That is why a 1,024 Wh power station that runs a 1,500 W heater for about 35 minutes can run a 100 W blanket for about 8 hours: roughly 13 times longer. The full space heater math is in Can a Portable Power Station Run a Space Heater?.

12 V blankets and the car outlet

Some heated blankets are made for 12 V car sockets. Plugging one into the power station’s 12 V car outlet skips the inverter, so you save the 10 W it would use. Check that the blanket’s watts fit the outlet: the 12 V car outlets on the units we cover are limited to roughly 120–126 W.

How to find your blanket’s real watts
Controller label: most controllers show volts, hertz and watts molded on the back or on a sticker.
Blanket tag: the sewn-in tag usually repeats the rating; on dual-control blankets, check both sides.
Manual or product page: brands such as Sunbeam list wattage in the specifications.
Plug-in watt meter: for the most accurate number, measure a full night on your usual setting and read the watt-hours in the morning. That total replaces the watts × hours in the formula.
Battery-friendly ways to stay warm, compared

Here is how much electricity common warming options need on a power station, using the same figures as our other guides:

Option	Power draw	Hours on a 1,024 Wh unit
Electric blanket, single	About 60 W	About 12 hours
Electric blanket, double	About 100 W	About 7.9 hours
Gas furnace with ECM blower (average)	About 99 W average	About 8 hours; see our furnace guide
Space heater, low setting	About 750 W	About 1.1 hours
Space heater, high setting	About 1,500 W	About 35 minutes

A blanket and a modern gas furnace use a similar amount of power, but the furnace needs a transfer switch or inlet installed by an electrician, while a blanket plugs straight into the power station.

Three real scenarios
Scenario	Setup	Math	Result
Couple, winter outage night	Queen blanket, both sides at 100 W, on a 2,048 Wh unit	1,741 Wh ÷ 210 W	About 8.3 hours: one full night
Solo camping, small unit	Single 60 W blanket on a 286 Wh unit	243 Wh ÷ 70 W	About 3.5 hours: enough to pre-warm the bed, not a whole night
Warmth plus Wi-Fi	100 W blanket + 15 W router on a 2,048 Wh unit	1,741 Wh ÷ 125 W	About 14 hours
Tips to make the charge last
Pre-heat, then turn it down. Warm the bed on high, then drop to a low setting for the night.
Use the lowest comfortable setting. Our table assumes full power; lower settings stretch the runtime.
Insulate around you. Close the bedroom door and use regular blankets under you and around you, but never pile anything on top of an electric blanket while it is on.
Charge fully before the storm so you start the night at 100%.
Keep the heater off. One hour of a 1,500 W heater costs as much energy as about 14 hours of a 100 W blanket.
Safety: use the blanket the way it was designed

The Electrical Safety Foundation International reports that heating pads and electric blankets cause almost 500 fires a year, almost all involving blankets more than ten years old. Its advice is simple: replace blankets with charred, frayed or cracked parts, never fold a blanket while it is on, and do not put anything on top of it, including other blankets or pets. Heating pads and electric blankets are not meant to be used at the same time.

Many blanket manuals also warn against using a heated blanket with infants, young children, people who cannot operate the controls, or anyone who is sensitive to heat. Always follow the warnings in your blanket’s manual.

A note from a physician

Electric blankets are not safe for everyone. People who may not feel heat well, such as some people with diabetes or nerve damage, people who cannot move easily, and infants and young children can be burned without noticing. For them, use layers and regular blankets instead, and always follow the blanket maker’s warnings. — Alejandro Rodríguez, MD

Common mistakes
Reading only one controller. Dual-control blankets draw power on both sides; add both labels.
Forgetting the inverter. The 10 W it uses is 10% on top of a 100 W blanket.
Bringing a space heater instead. On battery, a blanket gives far more warm hours per watt-hour.
Stacking bedding on top of the blanket. It can overheat; keep it uncovered.
Using an old, worn blanket. Replace it if it is more than ten years old or shows damage.

One person, one full night	EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus or Jackery Explorer 1000 v2	About 1 kWh: roughly 8 hours of a 100 W blanket
Two people, plus other essentials	Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2	2,048 Wh: a full night of a queen blanket on both sides

Frequently asked questions

For a 60 W single blanket, about 500 × 0.85 ÷ 70 = 6 hours at full power, and longer on a low setting. A 100 W blanket would run about 3.9 hours, so plan on a 1 kWh unit for a full night.

 How big a power station do I need for an electric blanket?
 Start with the night. A 150 W blanket averages about 75 W, so 8 hours use about 600 Wh. After inverter loss, you need about 700 Wh of battery for each night. Add a few small things and the number grows slowly: two phones charged at about 12 W for 2 hours each use about 48 Wh, and a 9 W bulb for 5 hours uses about 45 Wh.
 Here is how the size classes line up for the blanket alone. A 286 to 288 Wh unit gives about 3 to 3.5 hours. The 499 Wh Yeti 500 gives about 5.5 hours. A 1,000 Wh unit gives about 11 to 12 hours, and the 1,152 Wh BLUETTI AC180 about 13 hours. A 2,000 Wh unit gives about 23 to 24 hours, which is 2 nights.
 Bigger units stretch further. The BLUETTI Apex 300 runs the blanket for about 31 hours, 3 nights, and the Jackery HomePower 3000 for about 35 hours, 4 nights. The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus and EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 reach about 44 to 46 hours, 5 nights. For a blanket alone, that is more battery than most homes need.
 Why a blanket beats a space heater in an outage
 A blanket warms you, not the room. It draws about 150 W against 1,500 W for a space heater, and both cycle on and off about half the time. That makes the blanket average about 75 W and the heater about 750 W.
 The gap shows up fast. A 1,000 Wh unit runs the blanket for about 12 hours and a 1,500 W heater for about 1 hour. A 2,000 Wh unit runs the blanket for about 23 hours and the heater for about 2.5 hours. The 288 Wh units and the Yeti 500 cannot run the heater at all, because they stop at 300 to 600 W.
 If you want to heat a room, a station is the wrong tool and our space heater guide shows the limits. For one person in a cold house, a blanket and warm layers use a fraction of the energy.
 What if my blanket uses less than 150 W?
 Many blankets are rated lower, and some draw as little as 50 W. Our data only covers the 150 W model, so we give no numbers for other wattages. Runtimes scale with the draw: a blanket that uses less power runs longer on the same battery, and one that uses more runs shorter.
 To check yours, read the label for watts. If it lists volts and amps, multiply them. Then compare it to 150 W and adjust the hours up or down. Treat the result as a rough guide, because the controller setting and the room temperature change how often the heat cycles.
 What to look for in a station for a heated blanket
 Output is rarely the problem. The blanket needs only 150 W with no extra start-up surge, so all 20 stations in our table can run it. Pick on battery size, weight and how fast it refills.
 A UPS switch-over helps if you plug the blanket in all winter and want it to stay on when the grid drops. The Elite 100 V2, C1000 Gen 2 and Explorer 300 v2 list 10 ms, and the Explorer 2000 v2 lists 20 ms.
 Weight matters if the station moves between rooms. The Explorer 300 v2 is 8.2 lb, the Yeti 500 16.1 lb, the Elite 100 V2 25 lb and the Explorer 2000 v2 39.5 lb.
 Mistakes to avoid
 Sizing a battery for a space heater. Plan around the blanket, and treat any heater time as a short bonus.
 Running a CPAP and a blanket on a small unit without doing the sum. Together they average about 109 W. A 1,024 Wh unit lasts about 8 hours with both, right at the edge of one night. The Explorer 2000 v2 lasts about 16 hours, just short of two nights.
 Assuming the label wattage is the average. The controller cycles the heat, so the real average is about half. Check your own blanket's label before you size a battery.
 A power station should never be your only backup for a CPAP or any equipment you rely on to breathe. Treat it as a short bridge, and talk to your equipment supplier about outage plans. Register with your utility's medical-needs program as well.
 Safety
 Follow the blanket maker's instructions. Do not use a blanket that is folded, tucked in or damaged, and do not plug a damaged cord into the station.
 Keep the station dry and leave space around its vents. Never run a gas generator indoors. Never power your home by plugging a station into a wall outlet with a double-ended cord, because it can injure utility workers. If you want it to feed home circuits, have an electrician install a transfer switch or inlet.
 Common questions
 How long will a power station run an electric blanket? A 150 W blanket averages about 75 W. A 288 Wh unit runs it about 3 to 3.5 hours, a 1,000 Wh unit about 11 to 12 hours and a 2,000 Wh unit about 23 to 24 hours. Lower-watt blankets last longer. 
 What size power station do I need for an electric blanket? For one 8-hour night, you need about 700 Wh of battery, so a 1,024 Wh unit is the smallest that covers it. For two nights, look at a 2,000 Wh unit. The blanket's low output means any station can run it. 
 Can a 300 Wh power station run an electric blanket all night? No. A 286 to 288 Wh unit runs a 150 W blanket for about 3 to 3.5 hours. That covers an evening but not a night. The 499 Wh Yeti 500 reaches about 5.5 hours, still under one night. 
 Can I run a CPAP and an electric blanket at the same time? Yes, on any of our stations. Together they average about 109 W. A 1,024 Wh unit lasts about 8 hours and a 2,042 Wh unit about 16 hours. A station is a short bridge for a CPAP, never the only backup. 
 How long will a power station run a 50 W electric blanket? Longer than a 150 W model, because runtime scales with the draw. Our data only has the 150 W blanket, so we give no hours for 50 W. Check your blanket's label and adjust our hours up in proportion.

The important distinction is this: small battery heating products can warm a person, but a full room heater usually needs a much larger battery system such as a portable power station.
 Why Heaters Drain Batteries So Fast
 Electric heaters are different from laptops, routers, fridges, and CPAP machines. A fridge may use a high startup surge, then cycle off. A router may use 10–20W. A CPAP machine may use much less power if the humidifier is off. A heater keeps pulling hundreds or thousands of watts while it is actively producing heat.
 The simple comparison
 A 1,500W heater running for one hour uses 1.5 kWh of energy. Eight hours would use 12 kWh. That is far beyond what most portable power stations are designed to deliver overnight. A portable station is better used for targeted heating, short warm-up sessions, electric blankets, and essential backup loads.

 Safety Rules for Running a Heater from Battery Power
 A portable power station can be safer indoors than a fuel generator because it does not burn gasoline or produce exhaust, but the heater itself still needs respect. Electric heaters are high-wattage appliances and can create fire risk if misused.
 Do not treat a heater like a phone charger
 Do not run a heater unattended or while sleeping unless the heater manual clearly allows that use and the setup is safe.
 Keep the heater at least 3 feet away from bedding, curtains, paper, clothing, sofas, and other combustibles.
 Do not use damaged heaters, loose plugs, overheated cords, or questionable adapters.
 Do not exceed the power station’s continuous AC output rating.
 Do not rely on surge power for continuous heating.
 Keep the power station dry, ventilated, and away from heater airflow.
 Do not cover the power station vents.
 For additional heater safety guidance, see the CPSC portable electric heater safety bulletin .
 When a Portable Power Station Is the Right Tool
 A portable power station is a strong choice when you need clean, quiet indoor power for essential loads. It is especially useful for:
 Keeping phones, lights, routers, laptops, cameras, and medical devices powered.
 Running a fridge or freezer in planned intervals during an outage.
 Powering a CPAP machine with a properly sized backup setup.
 Running an electric blanket or heating pad for personal warmth.
 Using a space heater briefly while awake and nearby.
 Recharging from wall, car, or compatible solar panels when available.
 If your goal is to heat a whole room continuously for an entire night, a portable power station alone is usually not the most efficient solution. Use it as part of a smarter winter plan: reduce heat loss, warm the person first, keep critical devices running, and use the heater in short controlled sessions.
 FAQ: Portable Power Station Heater Runtime
 Can a portable power station run a space heater? 
 Yes, if the heater wattage is within the power station’s continuous AC output rating. A 750W heater can run on a properly rated model such as S1200 or S2400. A 1,500W heater needs a higher-output unit such as S2400 and will still drain the battery quickly.
 How long will a 2,000Wh power station run a 1,500W heater? 
 Using a 90% usable-energy estimate, a 2,083Wh power station such as UDPOWER S2400 can run a 1,500W heater for about 1.25 hours. Real runtime depends on the heater, temperature, fan behavior, and whether the heater cycles off.
 Can the UDPOWER S1200 run a 1,500W heater? 
 The S1200 is rated for 1,200W continuous AC output, so a 1,500W heater on high is not recommended. Use a lower heater setting under the rated output, such as 400W, 500W, 750W, or 1,000W, and test the actual wattage on the display.
 Is the UDPOWER S2400 better for heaters? 
 Yes. The S2400 has 2,400W continuous AC output and 2,083Wh capacity, so it is the better fit for higher-watt heaters. It can run a typical 1,500W heater, but runtime is still limited because electric heat uses a lot of energy.
 Are battery operated space heaters good for camping? 
 For tent camping, high-watt room-style battery operated space heaters are usually not efficient. A heated blanket, heated sleeping pad, warm sleeping bag, insulated tent setup, and a portable power station are usually more practical.
 What is better for battery backup: a space heater or electric blanket? 
 An electric blanket is usually much better for battery backup because it often uses 50–150W instead of 750–1,500W. It warms the person directly, so the same battery can last much longer.
 Can I sleep with a heater plugged into a portable power station? 
 Be very cautious. Follow the heater manual and safety instructions. Do not use damaged heaters, do not place heaters near bedding or curtains, and do not leave unsafe setups unattended. For overnight warmth, an electric blanket with proper safety features is usually a more battery-friendly option.
 Can solar panels keep a heater running all day? 
 Usually not by themselves. Solar panels can help recharge the power station during daylight, but a heater may use hundreds or thousands of watts continuously. Solar is more useful for restoring battery capacity between heater sessions and powering lower-watt essentials.

Can a Power Station Run an Electric Blanket? 11-12 Hours 
 Skip to content Will it run my…
 Can a power station run an electric blanket ?
 Updated October 10, 2026 
 Short answer
 Yes. A queen electric blanket is rated about 150 W and cycles to an average of about 75 W, so a 1,000 Wh power station runs it for about 11 to 12 hours, a full night with room to spare.
 Calculate your runtime

 Start-up 150 W 
 Runs 50 % of the time , about 75 W average 
 An electric blanket is the most efficient way to stay warm on battery. Sunbeam queen models are rated at 150 W, and most blankets fall between 100 and 200 W at full heat. The controller switches the heat on and off to hold your setting, so the element is not on all the time.
 There is no motor and no start-up surge, so any station in our table can run one. For a typical 8-hour night at 75 W average, you use about 600 Wh. After inverter losses, that is roughly 700 Wh of battery. A 288 Wh unit lasts about 3 hours, a 500 Wh unit about 5.5, a 1,000 Wh unit about 11 to 12, and a 2,000 Wh unit about 23.
 Compare that to a 1,500 W space heater, which averages about 750 W with its thermostat cycling and empties a 1,000 Wh unit in about an hour. A blanket uses about a tenth of the power. It warms you, not the room, so it will not keep pipes from freezing or a house warm. For that, a portable power station is the wrong tool.
 How long does each power station run an electric blanket ?
 At about 75 W on average, an electric blanket runs for about 3 hrs on the 286 Wh EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus, about 11 hrs to 12 hrs on a 1,000 Wh-class unit (998–1,070 Wh) and about 46 hrs on the 4,096 Wh EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3.
